title: Gallbladder Disease: Gallstones, Cholecystitis, and Their Complications
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains why gallstones form, why they come in three chemical types, and why the disease a stone causes depends on where it lodges. It covers acute calculous and acalculous cholecystitis, chronic cholecystitis with porcelain gallbladder and its link to adenocarcinoma, and the complications of a moving stone: biliary colic, choledocholithiasis, ascending cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, and Mirizzi syndrome. Board questions give the pain pattern, temperature, white cell count, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, and lipase and ask you to place the stone. If you know which duct is blocked and whether bacteria are present, each pattern follows from the anatomy.
prerequisites: Anatomy of the gallbladder, cystic duct, common hepatic duct, common bile duct, and ampulla of Vater
Bile composition and enterohepatic circulation of bile acids (GI-6)
Heme breakdown, bilirubin conjugation, and the conjugated versus unconjugated distinction
Cholecystokinin release and its actions on the gallbladder and sphincter of Oddi
Acute and chronic inflammation, dystrophic calcification, and metaplasia

connections.how: A duct stone causes conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with a cholestatic enzyme pattern, which must be separated from hepatocellular and hemolytic jaundice.
A stone at the ampulla blocks pancreatic drainage, making gallstones a leading cause of acute pancreatitis.
Chronic hemolysis in sickle cell disease and hereditary spherocytosis raises the bilirubin load and produces black pigment stones, often in young patients.
Enteric gram-negative rods infect obstructed bile, and flukes such as Clonorchis sinensis seed brown pigment stones in the ducts.
Long-standing stones and porcelain gallbladder are the main risk factors for gallbladder adenocarcinoma.

A water-soluble aggregate of bile salts and phospholipid (mainly lecithin) that carries cholesterol in bile.
A gel of mucin, cholesterol crystals, and calcium bilirubinate that forms in a stagnant gallbladder and can precede stones.
The insoluble calcium salt of unconjugated bilirubin that forms the bulk of pigment stones.
Steady visceral pain from transient cystic duct obstruction, lasting less than about 6 hours, without inflammation.
Arrest of deep inspiration when the examiner presses below the right costal margin and the inflamed gallbladder descends against the fingers.
Fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain, the classic presentation of ascending cholangitis.
A gallbladder whose scarred wall is calcified, typically after chronic cholecystitis.
An abnormal channel between the gallbladder and the bowel, most often the duodenum, formed when a stone erodes through adherent inflamed walls.
A bulge at the neck of the gallbladder where stones often impact.

blocks.text: Between meals the gallbladder stores hepatic bile and concentrates it, typically about fivefold, by absorbing Na+, Cl-, and water through its simple columnar epithelium. When fatty acids and amino acids enter the duodenum, I cells release cholecystokinin (CCK), which contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. The wall has mucosa, a thin smooth muscle layer, perimuscular connective tissue, and serosa, with no muscularis mucosae or submucosa, and it is supplied mainly by the cystic artery.

About 90% of acute cholecystitis is calculous, meaning it begins when a stone impacts in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck and stays there. Obstruction alone does not explain the inflammation, because the first injury is chemical: mucosal phospholipases convert lecithin in the trapped bile into lysolecithin, which damages the protective mucus layer and exposes the epithelium to the detergent action of concentrated bile salts, while prostaglandins released in the wall amplify the inflammation. Rising pressure in the distended organ compromises wall perfusion. Bacterial infection with enteric organisms such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and enterococci usually follows rather than starts the process.

blocks.title: Acute calculous cholecystitis
steps: Stone impacts in cystic duct or gallbladder neck
Trapped bile distends the gallbladder
Phospholipase converts lecithin to toxic lysolecithin
Mucus barrier lost; prostaglandins drive wall inflammation
Rising pressure reduces blood flow to the wall
Enteric bacteria secondarily infect the ischemic wall
blocks.caption: Chemical injury and ischemia come first; infection is a later step that drives empyema, gangrene, and perforation.

blocks.text: Each finding has a mechanism. Pain starts as poorly localized epigastric visceral pain carried by afferents entering the cord at about T6 to T9, then localizes to the right upper quadrant once the inflamed serosa touches parietal peritoneum, and it lasts longer than about 6 hours. It may be referred to the right scapula, or to the right shoulder when the diaphragm is irritated (phrenic nerve, C3 to C5). Cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF produce fever, often above 38 °C (100.4 °F), and a neutrophilic leukocytosis, commonly about 12,000 to 15,000/µL. In the Murphy sign, deep inspiration pushes the inflamed gallbladder down onto the examiner's fingers and the patient stops inhaling. Bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) are normal or only mildly raised from local edema; marked jaundice points to a duct stone or Mirizzi syndrome.

Imaging findings follow the same logic. Ultrasound shows the stone, a thickened wall, and pericholecystic fluid. In cholescintigraphy (HIDA scan), hepatocytes excrete a radiotracer into bile that reaches the duodenum but never fills the gallbladder because the cystic duct is blocked. Complications include empyema, gangrene, perforation with abscess, and emphysematous cholecystitis from gas-forming organisms such as Clostridium species, seen more often in people with diabetes.

blocks.title: Calculous versus acalculous cholecystitis
rows: Stasis and ischemia without a stone
Critically ill: sepsis, shock, burns, major trauma or surgery, prolonged fasting or TPN, mechanical ventilation
No CCK stimulus, so bile stagnates and concentrates; hypoperfusion injures the wall
Often settles if the stone disimpacts
Gangrene and perforation more frequent; mortality higher
blocks.caption: Acalculous disease is suspected when a critically ill patient develops fever, leukocytosis, or unexplained sepsis with a distended, thick-walled gallbladder and no stones.

blocks.predict: A patient with acute cholecystitis has a total bilirubin of 6 mg/dL and an ALP three times normal. Is the cystic duct stone enough to explain this?
blocks.explain: No. A cystic duct stone isolates only the gallbladder, while hepatic bile still drains through the common hepatic and common bile ducts, so marked cholestasis requires obstruction of the main duct: a common duct stone, cholangitis, or Mirizzi compression.

sections.title: Chronic cholecystitis, porcelain gallbladder, and gallbladder adenocarcinoma

blocks.text: Chronic cholecystitis is almost always associated with gallstones. It may follow repeated bouts of acute cholecystitis or develop gradually without a clear acute episode, and supersaturated bile itself probably contributes to mucosal injury. Bacteria, usually E. coli and enterococci, are cultured from the bile in only about one third of cases, so infection is not the main driver.

The pathology reflects long-term injury and repair. The wall is thickened by fibrosis and a mononuclear (lymphocyte and plasma cell) infiltrate, and the gallbladder may be contracted. Outpouchings of mucosal epithelium push through the muscle layer as Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses. Because the scarred wall contracts and empties poorly, patients describe recurrent biliary colic or vague postprandial right upper quadrant or epigastric discomfort rather than the fever and leukocytosis of acute disease.

Porcelain gallbladder is dystrophic calcification of this chronically inflamed, scarred wall. Dystrophic means calcium is deposited in damaged tissue while serum calcium is normal, the same process that calcifies old granulomas or scarred heart valves. On a plain radiograph or CT, the calcium outlines the gallbladder as a rim or stippled shell, and the organ often barely functions.

blocks.title: From stones to gallbladder adenocarcinoma
steps: Long-standing stones irritate the mucosa
Repeated inflammation and repair
Fibrosis and mural thickening
Dystrophic calcification: porcelain gallbladder
Metaplasia, then dysplasia, in chronically injured epithelium
Invasive adenocarcinoma
blocks.caption: Calcification and malignant change are separate outcomes of the same chronic injury; porcelain gallbladder marks that injury rather than causing cancer by itself.

blocks.text: Gallbladder adenocarcinoma is the most common malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. It is more common in women and in older adults, with high rates in some Native American, Chilean, and northern Indian populations, and most patients have gallstones. Chronic irritation drives a metaplasia, dysplasia, and carcinoma sequence. Porcelain gallbladder raises the risk, although modern series report a lower risk than older studies, and selective (incomplete) mucosal calcification appears riskier than diffuse calcification of the muscle layer. Other recognized risks include an anomalous pancreaticobiliary duct junction, which allows pancreatic juice to reflux into the bile, and chronic Salmonella Typhi carriage.

The tumor is usually silent until advanced, because early disease produces few symptoms or mimics ordinary biliary pain. The thin wall without a submucosa, and the hepatic surface that lies against the liver without serosa, allow early direct invasion of the liver. Spread to the cystic and hepatic hilar nodes and invasion of the common hepatic duct then cause obstructive jaundice, weight loss, and a right upper quadrant mass, which is why prognosis is poor.

sections.title: Cholesterol, black pigment, and brown pigment stones

blocks.text: Hepatic bile carries three lipids. Bile salts are secreted by the bile salt export pump (BSEP, ABCB11), phosphatidylcholine (lecithin) by the MDR3 flippase (ABCB4), and cholesterol by the ABCG5/ABCG8 transporter. Cholesterol is insoluble in water and stays dissolved only inside mixed micelles of bile salts and lecithin, or in lecithin vesicles. In Western countries about 80% of stones are cholesterol stones.

Cholesterol stones need four conditions acting together. First, bile becomes supersaturated because the liver secretes too much cholesterol or too few bile salts or phospholipid. Second, excess cholesterol leaves unstable vesicles that fuse and nucleate cholesterol monohydrate crystals. Third, gallbladder mucin forms a gel that traps the crystals. Fourth, gallbladder hypomotility keeps them in place long enough to grow. Supersaturation alone is common and harmless if the gallbladder empties well, which is why stasis matters so much.

blocks.title: Cholesterol stone formation
steps: More cholesterol or fewer bile salts and lecithin secreted
Bile becomes supersaturated with cholesterol
Unstable vesicles nucleate cholesterol monohydrate crystals
Mucin gel traps crystals as sludge
Hypomotile gallbladder retains them
Crystals aggregate into stones
blocks.caption: Supersaturation, nucleation, mucus hypersecretion, and stasis must coincide; any one alone rarely makes a stone.

blocks.title: Cholesterol stone risk factors and their mechanisms
rows: Estrogen increases hepatic cholesterol uptake and synthesis and its secretion into bile
Estrogen raises biliary cholesterol; progesterone relaxes smooth muscle and slows emptying
Increased hepatic cholesterol synthesis and biliary secretion
Rapid weight loss, prolonged fasting, TPN
Mobilized cholesterol enters bile; little fat intake means little CCK, so the gallbladder stagnates
Biliary cholesterol secretion rises and the bile acid pool shrinks
Inhibit cholesterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase, so less cholesterol becomes bile acid and more is secreted unchanged
Ancestry (some Native American and Mexican American groups) and ABCG8 variants
Inherited increase in biliary cholesterol secretion
blocks.caption: Every risk factor either raises cholesterol saturation, lowers bile salt or phospholipid output, or slows gallbladder emptying.

blocks.text: Pigment stones are made of calcium bilirubinate. Normal bile contains bilirubin mostly as water-soluble glucuronides, with only a little unconjugated bilirubin. Anything that raises unconjugated bilirubin in bile lets it bind calcium and precipitate.

Black pigment stones form in sterile gallbladder bile when the bilirubin load is high, as in chronic hemolysis (sickle cell disease, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia, mechanical heart valves) and cirrhosis. Gallstones in a child or young adult should prompt a search for hemolysis. Brown pigment stones form in infected ducts, including intrahepatic ducts. Bacterial beta-glucuronidase from E. coli and other enteric organisms deconjugates bilirubin glucuronides, and bacterial phospholipase releases fatty acids from lecithin, which form calcium soaps. Biliary parasites such as Clonorchis sinensis and Ascaris lumbricoides predispose to infection, so brown stones are more common in East Asia, and they can form in the ducts after cholecystectomy.

blocks.title: The three stone types
rows: Calcium bilirubinate with calcium soaps of fatty acids
blocks.caption: Black stones follow blood breakdown; brown stones follow bacteria in the ducts.

blocks.text: Ileal disease or resection, as in Crohn disease, also raises gallstone risk. Robbins groups it with pigment stones, because unabsorbed bile acids reaching the colon solubilize unconjugated bilirubin and increase its enterohepatic return; review books often list it under cholesterol stones, because a smaller bile salt pool favors supersaturation.

sections.title: Where the stone lodges decides the disease

blocks.text: Most gallstones never cause symptoms; when they do, ask which duct is blocked and whether bacteria are present. A cystic duct block isolates only the gallbladder, so bilirubin stays normal. A common bile duct block stops all bile flow, so conjugated bilirubin and ALP rise. Infection behind an obstruction adds fever and the risk of sepsis.

blocks.title: Gallstone complications by location
rows: Gallbladder contracts against a stone after a fatty meal; no inflammation
Steady (not colicky) pain under about 6 hours; normal labs
Pain over 6 hours, fever, Murphy sign, leukocytosis
Jaundice, high conjugated bilirubin, ALP, and GGT
Charcot triad; Reynolds pentad adds hypotension and confusion
Epigastric pain radiating to the back; lipase over 3 times normal
Stone erodes into duodenum, lodges in terminal ileum
Small bowel obstruction, air in the biliary tree
blocks.caption: Each added finding moves the diagnosis: pain alone, pain with fever, pain with jaundice, then all three.

blocks.text: Duct stones usually pass from the gallbladder, although brown stones can form in the duct itself. Water-soluble conjugated bilirubin spills into urine and darkens it, little reaches the gut, so stools pale, and retained bile salts cause pruritus. Prolonged obstruction impairs vitamin K absorption and prolongs the prothrombin time. Aminotransferases may spike briefly after acute obstruction, unlike the sustained rise of hepatitis. A scarred, stone-filled gallbladder rarely distends, so a palpable nontender gallbladder with jaundice (Courvoisier sign) suggests a tumor of the pancreatic head or distal bile duct instead.

blocks.title: Ascending cholangitis
steps: Stone obstructs the common bile duct
Bile stagnates; intraductal pressure rises
Enteric bacteria ascend and multiply
Pressure drives bacteria and endotoxin into the blood
Bacteremia: fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain
Septic shock, confusion, or liver abscess
blocks.caption: Obstruction, infection, and pressure together; usual organisms are E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides.

blocks.text: Gallstone pancreatitis follows small stones or sludge that pass the cystic duct and obstruct the ampulla, where the bile and pancreatic ducts usually share a channel, so small stones are riskier than large ones. Raised pancreatic duct pressure lets trypsinogen activate within acinar cells, starting autodigestion. An early rise in ALT favors a biliary over an alcoholic cause.

Gallstone ileus, despite its name, is a mechanical obstruction, typically in older women. Chronic inflammation fuses the gallbladder to the duodenum, and a large stone (usually over about 2.5 cm) erodes through as a cholecystoduodenal fistula, then lodges where the small bowel is narrowest, the terminal ileum near the ileocecal valve. Air entering through the fistula outlines the bile ducts (pneumobilia); a stone impacted in the duodenum or pylorus instead causes gastric outlet obstruction (Bouveret syndrome).

blocks.title: Placing the stone from the numbers
blocks.text: A 58-year-old woman has 2 days of right upper quadrant pain. Temperature is 39.2 °C (102.6 °F), WBC 17,000/µL, total bilirubin 4.8 mg/dL (reference about 0.3 to 1.2), mostly conjugated, ALP 380 U/L (reference about 40 to 130), lipase normal. Step 1: days of pain with fever and leukocytosis means inflammation, not colic. Step 2: conjugated bilirubin and ALP several times normal mean the main duct is obstructed, which a cystic duct stone cannot do. Step 3: obstruction plus fever and pain completes Charcot triad, so the answer is ascending cholangitis from choledocholithiasis. Step 4: normal lipase argues against pancreatitis. Added hypotension and confusion would make it Reynolds pentad.

blocks.predict: Why does gallstone ileus produce air in the bile ducts, while choledocholithiasis does not?
blocks.explain: The fistula opens the gallbladder to the gas-filled duodenum, so air refluxes into the ducts; in choledocholithiasis the sphincter of Oddi and the stone keep bowel gas out.

blocks.text: The cystic duct joins the common hepatic duct to form the common bile duct. The cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver bound the hepatocystic triangle (Calot triangle), which usually contains the cystic artery. In some people the cystic duct runs parallel to the common hepatic duct for a distance or joins it low, so the two share a wall and a common connective tissue sheath.

Mirizzi syndrome occurs when a stone impacted in the gallbladder neck (Hartmann pouch) or cystic duct, together with the inflammation around it, compresses the common hepatic duct from outside. No stone needs to be inside the main duct, yet hepatic bile cannot pass, so the patient develops the same conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, raised ALP and GGT, dark urine, and pale stools as in choledocholithiasis, often with the pain and fever of cholecystitis. Over time, pressure necrosis can erode the duct wall and create a cholecystobiliary (cholecystocholedochal) fistula, and the condition is graded by whether such a fistula has formed and how much of the duct wall it involves.

blocks.title: Mirizzi syndrome
steps: Large stone impacts in Hartmann pouch or cystic duct
Stone and surrounding inflammation press on common hepatic duct
Extrinsic narrowing blocks hepatic bile flow
Ducts above dilate; common bile duct below stays normal
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia and cholestatic enzyme pattern
Continued pressure may erode into the duct as a fistula
blocks.caption: The obstruction lies outside the duct, which explains why the duct below the compression is normal.

blocks.text: On imaging, the ducts above the compression are dilated, the common bile duct below is normal, and the stone sits in the gallbladder neck rather than in the duct. Because an extrinsic narrowing at the hepatic hilum can look like a tumor, Mirizzi syndrome is an important mimic of cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder carcinoma. Stagnant bile above the narrowing can also become infected and cause cholangitis.

blocks.title: Telling Mirizzi syndrome from its look-alikes
rows: Neck or cystic duct, pressing on common hepatic duct
Dilated, including common bile duct above the stone
Intrahepatic and common hepatic ducts dilated
blocks.caption: Mirizzi combines the stone position of cholecystitis with the laboratory pattern of a duct stone.

integration.text: Biochemistry sets the stone type: cholesterol stones reflect the balance of ABC transporters, bile acid synthesis by 7-alpha-hydroxylase, and the micelle, while pigment stones reflect heme turnover and whether bilirubin stays conjugated. Hematology and microbiology decide which pigment stone forms, black with hemolysis and brown with enteric bacteria or flukes. Physiology explains timing, because CCK released by a fatty meal contracts the gallbladder against a stone and fasting removes that stimulus and breeds sludge.

Anatomy then decides the clinical picture: cystic duct, common bile duct, ampulla, Calot triangle, and the duodenum next to the gallbladder predict colic, cholecystitis, jaundice, pancreatitis, Mirizzi syndrome, and gallstone ileus. Pathology supplies the outcomes of chemical injury, ischemia, fibrosis, dystrophic calcification, and carcinoma. These patterns have limits. Labs overlap, a stone can pass before testing and leave only a transient enzyme rise, and acalculous disease reminds you that stasis and ischemia can inflame the gallbladder without any stone.

summary: Cholesterol stones need supersaturated bile, crystal nucleation, trapping mucin, and a hypomotile gallbladder; estrogen, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, fasting, and fibrates act on one or more of these.
Black pigment stones form in sterile gallbladder bile with hemolysis or cirrhosis; brown pigment stones form in infected ducts through bacterial beta-glucuronidase.
Acute calculous cholecystitis begins as chemical injury from lysolecithin and prostaglandins behind an impacted cystic duct stone, with ischemia and secondary infection following.
Pain over about 6 hours with fever, leukocytosis, and Murphy sign means cholecystitis; the same pain under 6 hours with normal labs means biliary colic.
Acalculous cholecystitis arises from stasis and hypoperfusion in critically ill patients and more often progresses to gangrene and perforation.

Chronic cholecystitis causes a fibrotic wall with Rokitansky-Aschoff sinuses; dystrophic calcification produces porcelain gallbladder, which together with long-standing stones is linked to gallbladder adenocarcinoma.
A cystic duct stone leaves bilirubin normal; a common bile duct stone raises conjugated bilirubin and ALP, and with infection produces Charcot triad or Reynolds pentad.
Small stones at the ampulla cause gallstone pancreatitis; a large stone through a cholecystoduodenal fistula causes gallstone ileus at the terminal ileum with pneumobilia.
Mirizzi syndrome is extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone in the gallbladder neck or cystic duct, giving obstructive jaundice with a normal common bile duct below.

verify: Cancer risk of porcelain gallbladder: older series quoted high percentages and recent series report only a few percent; confirm the figure or wording NABNE expects.
Ileal disease or resection is grouped with pigment stones in Robbins but with cholesterol stones in many review books; confirm which classification NABNE items use.
Early ALT rise as a marker of biliary pancreatitis is often given with a threshold of about 150 U/L; the number was left out pending confirmation.
Proportion of acalculous cholecystitis (about 5 to 10%) and radiopacity percentages for stone types vary between sources.
Mirizzi syndrome classification systems (number of types and fistula grading) differ between sources; only the general principle is given.
